questions.stem: Sophia Greenwood, 69, is in an ED bay with 4 months of worsening breathlessness, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and swollen ankles. She had an anterior STEMI a year ago. You now examine her neck veins. How should you position her and measure the jugular venous pressure?
options: Lie her flat, then measure the height of the pulsation above the clavicle
Sit her at 90°, then measure the external jugular vein's height below the earlobe
Recline at 45°, head turned slightly left; measure vertical height above sternal angle
Recline at 45°, then measure the distance along the neck from the suprasternal notch
questions.why: The JVP is the vertical height of the right internal jugular pulsation above the sternal angle, with the patient at about 45° and the head turned slightly to the left. Normal is up to 3 to 4 cm. Sophia's is raised by 5 cm, which shows systemic venous congestion.
notes: Lying her flat would make her more breathless, and the clavicle is not the reference point; the sternal angle is used because it sits about 5 cm above the right atrium.
The external jugular can be kinked or affected by valves, so it is less reliable, and the earlobe is not a reference point for measuring the JVP.
The JVP is a vertical height measured from the sternal angle. A distance along the slope of the neck from the suprasternal notch overestimates it and has no reference range.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, has decompensated heart failure in the ED: RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, BP 144/84, bibasal crackles, oedema to mid-shins and pulmonary oedema on CXR. She has never taken a diuretic. Creatinine is 98 umol/L (eGFR 52). The nurse asks you for a drug, dose and route to treat her congestion now. Which order is most appropriate?
questions.why: In acute congestion, a patient who has never had a diuretic is given IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg. Then reassess breathing and urine output, and monitor fluid balance, daily weights and UEC with K and Mg.
notes: Bowel wall oedema makes oral absorption unreliable and slower, so for acute pulmonary oedema the IV route is used.
A beta-blocker should not be started while she is congested and decompensated. It is started at a low dose once she is euvolaemic and stable, if the echo shows HFrEF.
>Spironolactone is a weak diuretic with a slow onset. It is a long-term prognostic drug for HFrEF once she is stable and her potassium and renal function allow, not treatment for acute congestion.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, has heart failure after an anterior STEMI. She needs two extra pillows at night. In ED she slid down the trolley, and her RR rose from 26 to 28 and her SpO2 fell from 93% to 92%. What is the main mechanism of her worse breathlessness when she lies flat?
options: The abdominal contents push the diaphragm up and splint the lung bases
Lying flat lowers cardiac output by reducing venous return to the heart
Lying flat abolishes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and worsens V/Q matching
Blood shifts from legs and gut to the chest, raising pulmonary venous pressure
questions.why: Lying flat moves blood from the legs and gut into the chest and increases venous return. A failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra preload, so left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures rise and fluid leaks into the lung interstitium. Overnight reabsorption of leg oedema adds to this and causes PND.
notes: The diaphragm does rise slightly when supine, but the main problem in orthopnoea is pulmonary venous congestion. Diaphragm splinting is the mechanism in ascites or obesity.
Lying flat increases venous return rather than reducing it. The problem is a failing ventricle that cannot handle the extra preload, not a fall in output from too little filling.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is not abolished by posture, and V/Q mismatch does not explain why a raised preload brings on breathlessness in heart failure.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, had a STEMI treated with a stent 12 months ago. Today's ECG shows sinus tachycardia with pathological Q waves in V1 to V4, poor R wave progression and shallow T inversion in V2 to V4, all unchanged from her post-PCI ECG. Which coronary artery was most likely occluded in her previous infarct?
questions.why: V1 to V4 cover the septum and anterior wall of the LV, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. Losing this large area of muscle is a common cause of ischaemic cardiomyopathy and HFrEF.
notes: Occlusion of the right coronary artery usually gives an inferior infarct, with changes in II, III and aVF. It may also involve the RV or the posterior wall.
The left circumflex supplies the lateral wall. Its infarcts show in I, aVL and V5 to V6, or as posterior changes, not in V1 to V4.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and the posterior third of the septum. Its infarcts show inferiorly, not as anterior Q waves in V1 to V4.
